paragraphs: I would be wasting my readers’ time and my own if I tried to demonstrate how the general mediocrity of fortunes, the absence of excess wealth, the universal desire for comfort, and the constant effort everyone makes to obtain it cause the taste for the useful to outweigh the love of the beautiful in the human heart. Democratic nations, where all these conditions exist, will therefore cultivate the arts that make life easy rather than those whose aim is to adorn it. They will habitually prefer the useful to the beautiful, and they will demand that the beautiful also be useful. But I mean to go further. Having pointed out this first feature, I want to sketch several others.

In ages of privilege, it commonly happens that the practice of almost all the arts becomes a privilege, and that every profession is a separate path that not everyone is allowed to enter. Even when productive industry is free, the fixed character of aristocratic nations gradually separates all the people who practice the same art, until they form a distinct class, always made up of the same families. Its members all know one another, and a public opinion of their own and a kind of corporate pride soon arise among them. In a class or guild of this kind, each artisan has not only his fortune to make but also his reputation to protect. He is guided not only by his own interest, or even by that of his customer, but by that of the body to which he belongs. And the interest of that body is that each artisan should produce the best possible work. In aristocratic ages, then, the aim of the arts is to manufacture as well as possible, not as quickly or as cheaply as possible.

When, on the contrary, every profession is open to all, when a multitude of people are constantly entering and leaving it, and when its members are strangers to one another, indifferent, and so numerous that they hardly see one another, the social bond is destroyed. Each workman, standing alone, simply tries to earn as much money as he can at the least possible cost. The customer’s will is then his only limit. But at the same time a corresponding revolution takes place in the customer. In countries where wealth as well as power is concentrated in the hands of a few and stays there, the enjoyment of most of this world’s goods belongs to a small number of individuals, who are always the same. Necessity, public opinion, or moderate desires keep everyone else from enjoying them. Since this aristocratic class stays fixed at the pinnacle of greatness where it stands, neither shrinking nor growing, it is always moved by the same wants and affected by them in the same way. The men who make it up naturally draw from their superior, hereditary position a taste for what is extremely well made and durable. This shapes the general way the nation thinks about the arts. Among such a people it often happens that even the peasant would rather go without the thing he longs for than get it in an imperfect state. In aristocracies, then, craftsmen work for only a limited number of very demanding customers, and the profit they hope to make depends mainly on the perfection of their work.

This is no longer the case when all privileges have been abolished, ranks are mixed together, and people are forever rising or sinking on the ladder of society. Among a democratic people there are always a number of citizens whose inheritance is being divided up and is dwindling. Under more prosperous circumstances they acquired certain wants, which remain after the means of satisfying them are gone, and they anxiously look for some underhanded way of providing for them. On the other hand, democracies always have a large number of men whose fortunes are growing, but whose desires grow much faster than their fortunes. They gloat over the gifts of wealth in anticipation, long before they have the means to command them. Such men are eager to find some shortcut to these gratifications, which already seem almost within their reach. The combined result of these causes is that in democracies there are always a multitude of individuals whose wants exceed their means, and who are very willing to settle for an imperfect satisfaction rather than give up what they desire.

The artisan readily understands these passions, because he shares them. In an aristocracy he would try to sell his work at a high price to a few people. Now he sees that the quicker way to get rich is to sell at a low price to everyone. But there are only two ways of lowering the price of goods. The first is to discover a better, shorter, and more ingenious method of producing them. The second is to manufacture a larger quantity of goods that are nearly the same but of lower value. Among a democratic population, all the intellectual faculties of the workman are directed to these two objects. He strives to invent methods that will let him work not only better but also faster and more cheaply. Or, if he cannot manage that, he tries to reduce the intrinsic quality of what he makes, without making it entirely unfit for its intended use. When only the wealthy had watches, almost all of them were very good ones. Few watches are now made that are worth much, but everybody has one in his pocket. Thus the democratic principle not only tends to turn the human mind toward the useful arts, but it also leads the artisan to produce a quantity of imperfect goods more rapidly, and the consumer to be satisfied with those goods.

This does not mean that the arts in democracies are incapable of producing very admirable works when they are called for. That may occasionally happen, if customers appear who are willing to pay for time and effort. In this rivalry of every kind of industry, in the midst of this immense competition and these countless experiments, some excellent workmen emerge who reach the utmost limits of their craft. But they rarely have a chance to show what they can do. They are scrupulously sparing with their powers. They remain in a state of accomplished mediocrity, which condemns itself and, although it is perfectly able to shoot past the mark before it, aims only at what it hits. In aristocracies, by contrast, workmen always do all they can, and when they stop, it is because they have reached the limit of their skill.

When I arrive in a country and find some of the finest products of the arts there, I learn nothing from that fact about the social condition or the political constitution of the country. But if I see that the products of the arts are generally of inferior quality, very abundant, and very cheap, I am convinced that among that people privilege is declining, that ranks are beginning to mix, and that they will soon be completely confused.

The craftsmen of democratic ages strive not only to bring their useful products within reach of the whole community but also to give all their goods attractive qualities that they do not really have. In the confusion of all ranks, everyone hopes to appear what he is not, and makes great efforts to succeed. This feeling, which is only too natural to the human heart, does not originate in the democratic principle, but that principle applies it to material objects. Mimicking virtue belongs to every age, but the hypocrisy of luxury belongs more particularly to the ages of democracy.

To satisfy these new cravings of human vanity, the arts turn to every kind of imposture, and these devices sometimes go so far as to defeat their own purpose. Imitation diamonds are now made that can easily be mistaken for real ones. As soon as the art of making false diamonds reaches such a degree of perfection that they cannot be told apart from real ones, it is probable that both will be abandoned and become mere pebbles again.

This leads me to speak of the arts that are called the fine arts, to set them apart from the others. I do not believe that a democratic social condition and democratic institutions necessarily reduce the number of men who cultivate the fine arts. But these causes have a very powerful influence on the way the fine arts are cultivated. Many of those who had already acquired a taste for the fine arts are impoverished. On the other hand, many who are not yet rich begin to form that taste, at least by imitation. The number of consumers increases, but wealthy and demanding consumers become scarcer. Something similar to what I have already pointed out in the useful arts then takes place in the fine arts. Artists produce more works, but the merit of each work is lessened. No longer able to rise to what is great, they cultivate what is pretty and elegant, and appearance gets more attention than reality. In aristocracies a few great paintings are produced; in democratic countries, a vast number of insignificant ones. In the former, statues are cast in bronze; in the latter, they are modeled in plaster.

When I first arrived at New York, by the part of the Atlantic Ocean called the Narrows, I was surprised to see along the shore, some distance from the city, a considerable number of little palaces of white marble, several of them built on the models of ancient architecture. The next day I went to examine more closely the building that had particularly caught my attention, and I found that its walls were of whitewashed brick and its columns of painted wood. All the buildings I had admired the night before were of the same kind.

The social condition and the institutions of democracy also give certain distinctive tendencies to all the imitative arts, and these are easy to point out. They often draw the arts away from depicting the soul and fix them exclusively on depicting the body. They substitute the representation of motion and sensation for that of feeling and thought. In a word, they put the real in the place of the ideal. I doubt whether Raphael studied the minutest details of the mechanism of the human body as thoroughly as the draftsmen of our own time. He did not attach the same importance to rigorous accuracy on this point as they do, because he aspired to surpass nature. He sought to make of man something superior to man, and to make beauty itself more beautiful. David and his pupils, on the contrary, were as good anatomists as they were good painters. They depicted the models before their eyes wonderfully well, but they rarely imagined anything beyond them. They followed nature faithfully, while Raphael sought something better than nature. They have left us an exact portrait of man, but in his works Raphael gives a glimpse of the Divinity. This remark about the manner of treating a subject applies just as much to the choice of subject. The painters of the Middle Ages generally looked far above themselves, and far from their own time, for grand subjects that left their imagination an unbounded range. Our painters often use their talents to imitate exactly the details of private life, which they always have before their eyes, and they are forever copying trivial objects, whose originals are only too abundant in nature.
